subject: Will plyr help to analyze iterated random walk simulations?

messages.author: 27d6f297c0a55a1b
messages.subject: Will plyr help to analyze iterated random walk simulations?
parts:
Dear plyr folks,


I am sorry for this noob question and I promise I am currently reading
up on plyr’s features and usage. I read the announcement of plyr 1.6 on
the r-help list and I was wondering if plyr could help me.

I need to simulate how long a iterated random walk stays negativ [1].
Therefore I want to simulate a lot of (very long) random walks and look
when they cross 0. The code currently looks basically like this for a
normal random walk.

f1 <- function(n = 100000, # number of simulations
length = 100000) # length of iterated sum
{
z0 = 0L
z = rep(0L, times=length/2)

for (j in 1:n) {
x = sample(c(-1L, 1L), size=length, replace=TRUE)
if (x[1] >= 0 ) {
z0 = z0 + 1L
next
}

s = cumsum(x)
for (i in 1:length-1) {
if (s[i] < 0 && s[i + 1] >= 0) {
z[i/2] = z[i/2] + 1L
break
}
}
}
c(z0, z)
}

On r-help [1] it was suggested to use more vectorization to avoid the
for loops.

The problem when removing the outer for loop is, that when simulating
for example a million random walks with a length of one million the
matrix does not fit into the RAM and my system even freezes [2].

So I could do some basic calculations to look how much free memory the
system has only do that much samples of random walks of a certain length
so that they fit into memory, save the result and let a script call this
over and over again until I have the wanted amount of simulations.

Reading about plyr I understand it was written just for this purpose.
That means it splits the original data/matrix and processes small
pieces. Is that correct?

(I am in the process of removing the inner loop and replace it by R
commands and to optimize it further for example to use integers as
suggested to save memory [2].)


Thanks,

Paul


[1] https://stat.ethz.ch/pipermail/r-help/2011-July/285008.html
(beware that the posted code has errors)
[2] http://bugs.debian.org/cgi-bin/bugreport.cgi?bug=635832

You will get the hang of this with some practice. You are trying to
accumulate too much data.

Re-design this so you efficiently conduct 1 (as in one!) simulation,
collect the information you need, and then conduct the next one. Then
worry about looping later. To my eye, you do not need plyr, you just
need a regular old R lapply or sapply to get this done.

runOneSimulation <- function(x,y,z){
## figure out how long cumsum stays negative
res
}

This returns "res", the number of periods the sum is negative.

Once that works well, then it is easy to iterate. Hell, even a for
loop will suffice. You want to avoid idioms like

c(z0, z)

Because it calls a memory expanding operation over and over. Instead,
allocate the memory and fill it in.

How to do runOneSimulation efficiently? I think we would have to do
some testiing, the efficient approach will depend on the most likely
scenario. Your approach here allocates a giant vector, even if your
sum runs positive and the simulation stops. I would not do that.

I don't really think cumsum is the best way because it presupposes you
allocate that giant vector. I'm doing some testing. How about this.
It is not "vectorized", but it runs fast on my system and clarity is a
plus.


##Paul Johnson
## Aug. 4, 2011

## for R question about "how long does a sum of random
## walk stay negative

runOneSimulation <- function(){
counter <- 0
mysum <- 0
while (mysum <= 0){
mysum <- mysum + runif(1, min= -1,max= 1)
counter <- counter + 1
if (counter > 10000) break
}
#print(counter) ##testing
#print(mysum) ##testing
counter
}

set.seed(123123)
##test
runOneSimulation()
nsim <- 50000
myres <- numeric(nsim)

for ( i in 1:nsim){
myres[i] <- runOneSimulation()
}

hist(myres)
